raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old female patient presented with chest and back pain accompanied by fever, approximately 38.2 C, about 1 month prior to hospital admission, with normal limb mobility at that time. The local hospital initially diagnosed her with gallstones and cholecystitis, and she underwent cholecystectomy and received anti-infective treatment. Post-surgery, her temperature improved, but the pain persisted. She revisited the local hospital due to unrelieved pain, where she was considered to have a gastric ulcer and was treated with proton pump inhibitors among other medications, yet without symptom improvement. Two days before presenting to our hospital for further treatment, the patient experienced a gradual decrease in bilateral lower limb strength. During her stay, she had intermittent fever, peaking around 38.2 C, with no significant gastrointestinal symptoms. Emergency CT indicated a thoracic vertebral fracture at T6/T7 (Figure 1), suspected to be caused by vertebral infection. Subsequently, the patient was admitted to the orthopedics department. Physical examination upon admission revealed normal development, good nutritional status, natural facial expression, and moderate body build. The patient was alert and cooperative during the examination, with primary positive findings including loss of pain and touch sensation below the level of the xiphoid process, grade 0 strength in both lower limbs, positive bilateral Babinski sign, loss of saddle area touch sensation, and absence of the anal reflex. Admission tests showed a white blood cell count of 15.41x10^9/L, monocytes at 0.881x10^9/L, lymphocytes at 2.01x10^9/L, neutrophils at 12.971x10^9/L, C-reactive protein at 131.8 mg/L, and a temperature of 37.4 C. Considering the patient's test results and local epidemiological investigation, the diagnosis was considered to be an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and a treatment regimen primarily consisting of anti-tuberculosis drugs (levofloxacin, isoniazid, amikacin, rifampicin, ethionamide, and pyrazinamide) was initiated. Concurrently, related surgical examinations were completed, and on the third day of admission, surgery was performed (posterior spinal canal decompression with internal fixation by pedicle screw and lateral bone grafting), along with the placement of a wound drainage tube, and the excised tissue was sent for culture. Based on intraoperative findings, the doctor suspected a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and the anti-infective treatment regimen was adjusted to cefoperazone-sulbactam plus vancomycin.
On the fourth day of admission, 65 reads were identified as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and 19 reads were identified as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, and this result was also supported by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) verification. Based on the results of domestic epidemiological investigations, the anti-infection treatment plan was adjusted to ceftriaxone. The patient's temperature and inflammatory markers showed a trend of improvement, and she was subsequently transferred to a local hospital for continued treatment. Approximately 6 months later, follow-up revealed no fever, and stool culture and agglutination tests were negative, and no clinical sign of recurrence was observed in the spine (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old female presented with a 1-month history of chest and back pain with fever (~38.2 °C), and progressive bilateral lower limb weakness over 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began approximately 1 month prior to admission with chest and back pain accompanied by fever peaking around 38.2 °C, with normal limb mobility at that time. A local hospital diagnosed gallstones and cholecystitis; she underwent cholecystectomy and received anti-infective treatment, resulting in temperature improvement but persistent pain. She re-presented to the local hospital and was treated for suspected gastric ulcer with proton pump inhibitors without benefit. Two days prior to current admission, she developed progressive weakness in both lower limbs. Throughout her illness, she experienced intermittent fever peaking at 38.2 °C without significant gastrointestinal symptoms. Emergency CT revealed a thoracic vertebral fracture at T6/T7 concerning for vertebral infection, prompting orthopedic admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underwent cholecystectomy with anti-infective therapy for gallstones and cholecystitis 1 month prior; treated with proton pump inhibitors for presumed gastric ulcer. No other medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness, sensory loss below chest level, chest and back pain. Denies significant gastrointestinal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Alert, cooperative, well-nourished, moderate build, natural facial expression. Body temperature on admission 37.4 °C. Neurological examination revealed complete loss of pain and light touch sensation below the xiphoid process level, grade 0/5 muscle strength in bilateral lower limbs, positive bilateral Babinski sign, loss of saddle sensation, and absence of the anal reflex.
objective.routine_investigations: Body temperature 37.4 °C. White blood cell count 15.41 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 12.971 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 2.01 x 10^9/L, monocytes 0.881 x 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 131.8 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency CT showed a thoracic vertebral fracture at T6/T7 suspicious for vertebral infection. The patient underwent posterior spinal canal decompression with internal fixation via pedicle screws and lateral bone grafting with wound drainage on hospital day 3, with excised vertebral tissue submitted for microbiological culture and molecular analysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hematogenous spondylodiscitis / vertebral osteomyelitis with pathological fracture at T6/T7 and spinal cord compression caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi co-infection, confirmed on hospital day 4 by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (65 reads of S. Typhimurium and 19 reads of S. Typhi) and verified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of resected vertebral tissue. Suspected Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (initially treated empirically with levofloxacin, isoniazid, amikacin, rifampicin, ethionamide, and pyrazinamide) and intraoperatively suspected Staphylococcus aureus infection (empirically treated with cefoperazone-sulbactam plus vancomycin) were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Following molecular pathogen confirmation on day 4, antimicrobial therapy was targeted to intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient showed progressive clinical improvement with normalization of temperature and down-trending inflammatory markers, and was transferred to a local hospital for convalescent rehabilitation and antibiotic completion. At approximately 6 months follow-up, she was afebrile, stool cultures and agglutination tests were negative, and spinal imaging confirmed no clinical recurrence.
